title: Electric shock (low voltage household current)
summary: Electric shocks can cause burns where the current enters and leaves the body, and can disturb heart rhythm. Hidden internal damage is possible even when the skin looks fine.
steps: Do not touch the person while they are still in contact with the electricity. Switch off the power at the mains first if you can.

If you cannot switch off the power, stand on a dry, non-conducting surface (rubber mat, dry wood) and push them away from the source using a dry wooden stick or broom handle — never anything metal or wet.
Once safely disconnected, check if they are breathing and responsive.
Cool any visible burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes (treat as a thermal burn).
Cover burns loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth.
Keep the person warm and reassured while waiting for medical help.
Have them assessed even if they feel fine — heart rhythm and deep tissue damage may not show right away.
avoid: Do not touch a person still in contact with an electrical source — you will be shocked too.
Do not use water or metal objects to push them away from a live source.
Do not assume a small burn means a small injury — internal damage can be hidden.
Do not let them eat or drink in case treatment is needed.
whenToEscalate: Always — every electric shock that causes any burn, loss of consciousness, palpitations, muscle pain, or even a brief tingle that knocked them off their feet needs medical review.
Emergency immediately if they are unconscious, having chest pain or palpitations, breathing oddly, or have widespread burns.
High-voltage shocks (power lines, industrial sources) — always an emergency, large hidden injuries are typical.
specialty: Emergency department for assessment; burns unit if large burns.
